e4: Grabs the centre, opens lines for the queen and the light-squared bishop. The most popular first move at every level.
d4: Takes the centre with a pawn that is already protected by the queen. Games tend to be more strategic than after 1.e4.
c4: The English Opening: controls d5 from the side and keeps White's plans flexible.
Nf3: Develops a knight and stops ...e5. Often transposes to 1.d4 or 1.c4 openings.
g3: Prepares a kingside fianchetto with Bg2, aiming the bishop down the long diagonal.
b3: Prepares Bb2 to pressure the long diagonal towards Black's kingside.
f4: The Bird Opening: fights for e5 and can lead to sharp kingside play, but slightly weakens White's king.
e4 c5: The Sicilian Defence. Black fights for d4 from the side and creates an unbalanced position.
e4 e5: The classical reply: Black claims an equal share of the centre.
e4 e6: The French Defence. Black prepares ...d5 with a solid but slightly cramped position.
e4 c6: The Caro-Kann Defence. Black prepares ...d5 without blocking the light-squared bishop.
e4 d5: The Scandinavian Defence: Black challenges the e4 pawn immediately.
e4 d6: The Pirc set-up: Black lets White build a centre and plans to attack it later.
e4 Nf6: Alekhine's Defence: the knight invites White's pawns forward to become targets.
e4 g6: The Modern Defence: a fianchetto first, with the centre fight postponed.
e4 Nc6: The Nimzowitsch Defence: develops and pressures d4, a rare but playable choice.
e4 c5 Nf3: The main line: develops and prepares d4 to open the position.
e4 c5 Nc3: Prepares the Closed Sicilian (g3, Bg2) or the Grand Prix attack with f4.
e4 c5 c3: The Alapin: prepares d4 so White can recapture with a pawn and keep a big centre.
e4 c5 d4: The Smith-Morra idea: White offers a pawn for quick development.
e4 c5 Nf3 d6: Prepares ...Nf6 without allowing e5, heading for the Najdorf or Dragon.
e4 c5 Nf3 Nc6: Develops and controls d4 and e5; keeps several set-ups available.
e4 c5 Nf3 e6: Keeps a solid pawn chain and frees the dark-squared bishop; leads to the Taimanov, Kan or Paulsen.
e4 c5 Nf3 g6: The Hyperaccelerated Dragon: the bishop goes to g7 before ...Nc6 or ...d6.
e4 c5 Nf3 d6 d4: Opens the centre. Black usually takes on d4 and gets the half-open c-file in return.
e4 c5 Nf3 d6 d4 cxd4: Black trades a wing pawn for a centre pawn.
e4 c5 Nf3 d6 d4 cxd4 Nxd4: Recaptures and centralises the knight. White has more space; Black has the c-file.
e4 c5 Nf3 d6 d4 cxd4 Nxd4 Nf6: Attacks e4 so that White has to spend a move defending it.
e4 c5 Nf3 d6 d4 cxd4 Nxd4 Nf6 Nc3: Defends e4 with development. Now Black chooses: ...a6 (Najdorf), ...g6 (Dragon), ...Nc6 (Classical) or ...e6 (Scheveningen).
e4 c5 Nf3 d6 d4 cxd4 Nxd4 Nf6 Nc3 a6: The Najdorf: a useful waiting move that stops Nb5 and Bb5 and prepares ...e5 or ...b5.
e4 c5 Nf3 d6 d4 cxd4 Nxd4 Nf6 Nc3 g6: The Dragon: the bishop on g7 bites down the long diagonal.
e4 c5 Nf3 Nc6 d4: Opens the centre, the most principled answer.
e4 c5 Nf3 Nc6 d4 cxd4 Nxd4: Recaptures with the knight, keeping the open centre.
e4 c5 Nf3 e6 d4: Opens the centre; Black usually takes and keeps flexible.
e4 c5 Nf3 e6 d4 cxd4 Nxd4: Centralises the knight and keeps an edge in space.
e4 e5 Nf3: Develops with tempo by attacking e5.
e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6: Defends e5 while developing, the most natural reply.
e4 e5 Nf3 Nf6: The Petroff: Black counter-attacks e4 instead of defending e5.
e4 e5 Nf3 d6: The Philidor: a solid pawn defence of e5, though it is a little passive.
e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bb5: The Ruy Lopez: pressure on the knight that defends e5.
e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bc4: The Italian Game: the bishop eyes f7, Black's weakest square.
e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 d4: The Scotch: opens the centre straight away.
e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bc4 Bc5: The Giuoco Piano: Black mirrors White and points the bishop at f2.
e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bc4 Nf6: The Two Knights: Black counter-attacks e4 rather than waiting.
e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bc4 Bc5 c3: Prepares d4 to build a big pawn centre.
e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bc4 Bc5 c3 Nf6: Hits e4, so White has to decide between d3 (slow build-up) and d4 (open fight).
e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bc4 Bc5 c3 Nf6 d3: The modern Giuoco Pianissimo: keep e4 protected and manoeuvre slowly.
e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bc4 Nf6 d3: A calm defence of e4 that avoids the sharp lines after Ng5.
e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bb5 a6: The Morphy Defence: asks the bishop a question right away.
e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bb5 a6 Ba4: Keeps the pin on the knight; taking on c6 is also playable.
e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bb5 Nf6: The Berlin Defence: solid and famous for its endgame lines.
e4 e6 d4: Takes the full centre. Black will strike with ...d5.
e4 e6 d4 d5: Challenges e4. White must defend, push or exchange.
e4 e6 d4 d5 Nc3: Defends e4 with development and keeps tension.
e4 e6 d4 d5 e5: The Advance: grabs space; Black hits the chain with ...c5.
e4 e6 d4 d5 Nd2: The Tarrasch: avoids the pin from ...Bb4.
e4 e6 d4 d5 exd5: The Exchange: a symmetrical, quiet structure.
e4 c6 d4: Takes the centre. Black follows up with ...d5.
e4 c6 d4 d5: Challenges e4 with the c6 pawn ready to support d5.
e4 c6 d4 d5 Nc3: Defends e4. After ...dxe4 Nxe4 Black usually develops the bishop with ...Bf5.
e4 c6 d4 d5 e5: The Advance: gains space; Black develops the bishop to f5 before ...e6.
e4 c6 d4 d5 exd5: The Exchange: often followed by Bd3 and c3.
e4 d5 exd5: Takes the pawn. Black usually recaptures with the queen.
e4 d5 exd5 Qxd5: Recaptures, accepting that the queen comes out early.
e4 d5 exd5 Qxd5 Nc3: Develops and gains a tempo on the queen.
d4 d5: Mirrors White and stakes a claim in the centre.
d4 Nf6: Flexible: controls e4 and keeps every Indian defence available.
d4 d5 c4: The Queen's Gambit: offers a wing pawn to win control of the centre.
d4 d5 c4 e6: The Queen's Gambit Declined: solid, holds d5 with a pawn.
d4 d5 c4 c6: The Slav: holds d5 and keeps the light-squared bishop free.
d4 d5 c4 dxc4: The Queen's Gambit Accepted: Black gives up the centre for quick development.
d4 Nf6 c4: Takes more space and keeps White's options open.
d4 Nf6 c4 g6: Heads for the King's Indian or the Grünfeld.
d4 d5 Nf3: A flexible developing move, common in the London System.
d4 d5 Bf4: The London System: a solid set-up that can be played against almost anything.
c4 e5: The Reversed Sicilian: Black takes the centre on the other side.
c4 Nf6: Flexible: Black keeps the option of ...e5, ...e6 or ...g6.
c4 c5: The Symmetrical English: Black copies White and fights for d4.
